properties.name: A new sentence claiming the software refuses something is asserted somewhere before it ships
properties.statement:
**THE RULE.** When you write a sentence in a served tool description, skill or message that says the software REFUSES, CANNOT, or NEVER does something — make sure something asserts it before you commit. Usually that means checking a test already covers it; sometimes it means writing one line.

**IT APPLIES TO NEW AND REWORDED SENTENCES ONLY. IT IS NEVER RETROACTIVE**, and that is a ruling rather than an omission. ~100 such claims already stand and are ~98% true; backfilling them would write a hundred tests to catch perhaps two errors, and — the decisive half — it would address a cause that does not exist. A test written today cannot catch a sentence that was already false when it was committed; it documents whatever the code does now, which is a different act wearing the same clothes.

🛑 **ADVICE, NOT A GATE — `enforced: false`, and Anthony chose it deliberately on 2026-09-02 rather than leaving it unstated.** A gate can only catch claims it can FIND, and finding them needs the same keyword classifier used to size this rule: it proposed 197 candidates and reading 25 of them put the true figure near half. A check that misfires roughly one time in two is one people learn to skim, which is the failure `acknowledge_gap`'s own description warns about — *a list that can never reach zero gets skimmed*. Turning this into a red build would trade a real habit for an ignored one.

**WHAT WOULD CHANGE THAT.** If the classifier can be made precise enough to name new refusal claims in a diff with few false positives, the warn-in-CI form becomes available: print what it found, never fail. That was the option not taken, and it is the one to revisit — not the gate.

**WHY THIS RULE AND NOT "BE MORE CAREFUL".** Measured over the six known-false sentences: FOUR WERE FALSE THE DAY THEY WERE WRITTEN. In `loop_status` the counter and the claim it cannot support sit in ONE COMMIT, 57 LINES APART. In `unresolved_setup` the message announced "nothing follows through" while the loop had no condition at all. The authors had the code in front of them. Care is not the missing ingredient — a comparison is, and nothing forces one at the moment of writing.

The session that NAMED this class then came within one edit of adding to it: having fixed the gap-replay guard, both tool descriptions still carried the warning describing the behaviour just removed. It took a deliberate second pass to catch. That is the strongest available evidence that vigilance does not scale here — and it is also the honest limit of an unenforced rule, which asks for exactly that vigilance.

**WHAT IT COSTS.** ~6.5 new claims per week in steady state — a little over one per working day. During a burst of new tools it reached ~24/week in the 30 days to 2026-09-02, which is heaviest exactly when tools are being added fastest.

**THE AGREED NARROWING IF IT BITES:** keep hard REFUSALS (`is refused`, `cannot`) and drop the softer `never` / `nothing` forms. Refusals are what an agent acts on and are the cheapest to assert.

**WHAT GOOD LOOKS LIKE.** `loop_status`'s "an unknown contributor_id is REFUSED" has a test (`an_unknown_contributor_is_refused_rather_than_answered_with_an_empty_list`). It has been true since the day it shipped and cannot quietly become false. It is the only claim among those checked that is structurally protected, and it is the model.

**WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT.** Not a documentation-accuracy rule — advice to the reader ("never guess the node type") asserts nothing about the code and is out of scope. Not a ban on prose: this project's own field reports name the prose as the best thing about it, and the point is to keep it trustworthy, not to thin it out.

SOURCE: `dec:idea-the-load-bearing-prose-is-unchecked-against-the-code-it-describes`, settled by Anthony 2026-09-02, on `fact:the-prose-does-not-rot-it-is-born-false` and `fact:the-cost-of-pinning-refusal-claims-is-affordable-forward-and-pointless-backward`.
